title: Music Brings Joy to Veterans in Hospital
summary: Dante Ciolfi opens his guitar case in a hospital in Washington, D.C. He is going to play songs for patients. Ciolfi is a volunteer with Musicians On Call, a group that brings live music to hospital patients all over the country. Ellen Morris is another volunteer. She leads the musicians from room to room. At the hospice wing, she knocks on a door. 'I have my friend Dante here that would love to play a song for you today,' she says. The first patient is Lawrence Ludden, a 93-year-old Army veteran. Ciolfi sings 'Desperado' by the Eagles. Ludden smiles and claps. Next, Ciolfi plays for John Fay, a Marine veteran who cannot speak. Fay taps his heart as he listens. Then Sidney Nichols, an Air Force veteran, hears 'Crazy Love' and starts to sing along. 'I like it,' he says. Since this story was reported, Sidney Nichols has died. Musicians On Call has played for more than a million patients since 1999. Ciolfi says playing a song is one tiny thing he can do for veterans.
why_it_matters: Music can lift your mood when you feel sick or lonely, and playing a song for someone is a simple way to make their day better.

background_read: Musicians On Call is a group that brings live music to hospital patients all over the country.
Its volunteers play songs for patients, including veterans who are in the hospital.
Music can make a hard day in the hospital feel a little brighter, and a familiar song can make patients smile and sing along.
Article_Structure: WHO: Dante Ciolfi, a volunteer musician with Musicians On Call, and Ellen Morris, who leads the musicians from room to room.
WHAT: Volunteer musicians play live music for hospital patients, including veterans like Lawrence Ludden, John Fay, and Sidney Nichols.
WHERE: In a hospital in Washington, D.C., including the hospice wing.
WHY: Because live music can bring comfort and joy to people who are sick and far from home.
